title: Inverse problems are exponentially harder than forward evolution

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Inverse problems are exponentially harder than forward evolution

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: In almost any system whose behavior seems complex there is, in a fundamental sense, an almost exponential gap between the effort needed to compute behavior from given initial conditions and the effort needed to determine which initial conditions, if any, produce given behavior.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: there really can in some fundamental sense be an almost exponential difference in the amount of computational effort needed to find the behavior of a system with given particular initial conditions, and to solve the inverse problem of determining which if any initial conditions yield particular behavior.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 12, “The Principle of Computational Equivalence”; section “Undecidability and Intractability” (from p. 753), p. 771. Scope: systems with complex behavior, including cellular automata

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch12-29: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.49

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Restricted inverse problems are testable with public computation and sometimes proof. The near-universal claim cannot be resolved without a sampling measure and general lower-bound techniques.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For specified system ensembles, benchmark optimal forward and inverse algorithms under common encodings and prove lower bounds where possible. Polynomial inverse algorithms refute the gap for individual families, while exponential lower bounds confirm it only for the formalized families.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The gap depends strongly on output and input encodings.

"Almost any" has no defined ensemble.

Algorithm benchmarks do not establish optimal lower bounds.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Forward evolution of a simple cellular automaton is cheap, and the corresponding bounded inverse problem sits in NP, so the shape of the gap can be studied with ordinary simulation. What remains open is an almost exponential separation for almost any complex-looking system. That is a general lower-bound claim, and the cost of a particular search algorithm is weak evidence that every algorithm is slow.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For a concrete rule, measure steps to evolve a given initial condition for time t against steps to decide whether any initial condition yields a stated output. A proved superpolynomial separation confirms the gap for that system; a polynomial inverse algorithm refutes it there. A sample of rules is only a proxy for almost any complex-looking system.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
A proved gap for one system leaves the universal quantifier open.

Almost any complex-looking system is not a defined class.

Timing exhaustive search measures one algorithm, not the best algorithm.
